transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-19
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~47 mins
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonas Reed (Redwood SE), Amir Soliman (Redwood), Lena Ortiz (AxiomGrid, CTO), Marco Chen (AxiomGrid, SRE), Priya Rao (AxiomGrid, ML Eng Lead), Daniel Voss (AxiomGrid, Security)

[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick intros? I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood Dedicated team. Jonas and Amir with me, they'll handle the technical bits.
[00:10] Lena: Hey all, Lena here. High level: we're evaluating options to move core inference off our self-hosted cluster. Need isolation and predictable cost.
[00:20] Marco: Marco here, SRE. Primary ask is how we keep noisy neighbors out, prewarm strategies, and burst handling. We have production traffic that spikes 6x during batch pricing runs.
[00:32] Jonas: Great, that aligns with what we usually see. Quick note — we'll talk about prewarming, warm pools, and fallback tiers. AxiomGrid, do you have committed qps numbers or token rates?
[00:45] Priya: We're still modeling. At baseline, 200 QPS for short prompts, but 1k QPS during weekend batch jobs. Latency target p95 is 200–250ms for our customer-facing endpoints.
[00:58] Amir: Okay, important detail — are those short generative prompts or longer context? Sequence length affects kernel selection and throughput.
[01:10] Priya: Mostly short, 128 tokens on average. Some longer evaluation runs to 1k tokens but those are less frequent.
[01:22] Daniel: On security side, SOC2 is must-have. We also need tenant-level audit logs, KMS integration, and SSO via SAML.
[01:35] Maya: Yep, Redwood Dedicated supports KMS + customer-managed keys in Private, but Dedicated can also integrate with enterprise KMS via connectors. We'll share SOC2 docs.
[01:46] Lena: Can you walk through isolation models? We want physical tenancy or at least strong soft isolation; noisy neighbor risk is our top worry.
[01:58] Jonas: Sure — Dedicated offers reserved GPU pools per customer. There are a few topology options: full tenant fencing (single-tenant nodes), soft multi-tenant within a reserved pool (tenant sharding by instance), and hybrid where critical routes get fenced resources and lower-tier traffic uses shared capacity.
[02:20] Jonas: For AxiomGrid's p95 goal, fencing the critical customer-facing route is recommended. We can do hot pools for prewarm.
[02:32] Marco: How does hot pooling actually work? Is it a pool of preloaded KV caches?
[02:40] Jonas: Yeah we prewarm model weights and local KV caches to reduce cold-starts. There are strategies: keep N prewarmed slots, or use adaptive prewarm where we scale based on recent traffic. There's tradeoff in cost vs tail latency.
[02:55] Priya: For us, tail latency matters more than a few extra dollars, at least for the critical route. For lower-priority batch jobs, we can accept higher latency.
[03:08] Maya: Makes sense. On burst — Redwood Dedicated supports burst to a reserved warm pool or a cross-region fallback to hosted capacity if local exhausted. How predictable does the burst need to be?
[03:20] Lena: We need an SLA for critical route: 99.9% availability and p95 latency under 250ms. Burst can be best-effort for non-critical traffic.
[03:33] Marco: Another question: preemption or eviction policies. If we do hybrid, how do you protect isolated nodes from preemption?
[03:44] Jonas: Isolated nodes — no preemption, they're reserved. Shared warm pools can be preempted at high system pressure, but our routing will fallback to other model variants or hosted fallbacks.
[03:57] Daniel: On auditability — we need per-request logs and retention controls. Can we pull logs into our SIEM?
[04:07] Amir: Yes — Redwood can stream request traces and token-level cost metadata to your logging endpoint; retention and export configs are configurable.
[04:16] Lena: Pricing — ballpark numbers? We need to size the reserved pool first.
[04:23] Maya: We'll send a pricing sheet but to ballpark: reserved nodes priced per-GPU per-month, with options for committed throughput packs. Burst is charged differently, with a blended rate for on-demand overflow. We'll include example scenarios.
[04:38] Priya: For benchmarking — what's the recommended approach? We're worried about perf delta between your hosted optimized kernels vs our on-prem runs.
[04:47] Jonas: We can run a benchmark on Redwood Dedicated with your prompt set. Recommended: 1) a short smoke test on small subset, 2) full load test to 1k QPS with mixture of prompt lengths, 3) latency distribution capture (p50/p95/p99) and token cost. We'll provide a runbook.
[05:10] Marco: Network — we need VPC peering and to control egress. Can you support private link or VPC peering?
[05:18] Maya: Yes. Dedicated in customer VPC or Private deployment supports VPC peering and private endpoints. We'll want your network diagram.
[05:26] Daniel: What about encryption keys? KMS/HSM options?
[05:30] Amir: Dedicated can integrate with customer KMS; in Private you can bring-your-own HSM. For Dedicated we support envelope encryption with your KMS in your cloud region.
[05:39] Lena: Is there an option to run entirely on-prem? We may have a portion of workloads that must be air-gapped.
[05:46] Jonas: That's Redwood Private — on-prem appliance or VPC package. It's a different product but same API surface. We can discuss hybrid setups where critical data stays Private and others run on Dedicated.
[06:00] Priya: A concern — quantization. We use some fp16 models. What's the impact on latency/quality if you recommend int8 quantized variants?
[06:10] Amir: Quantization gives big speedups and cost reductions. We do quality regressions testing per prompt set. For critical routes we recommend running evals before switching. Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization profile and track regressions.
[06:25] Lena: Do you support automatic rollbacks if quality drops?
[06:28] Jonas: Yes, rollouts and automatic fallback policies exist — you can canary a quantized variant and if evals show regressions, traffic rolls back.
[06:36] Marco: On the topic of fallbacks, does Redwood support function/tool calling or tool restrictions across model variants?
[06:43] Amir: Tool calls are supported, but tool integration and access controls are configured at route level. You can restrict certain functions to specific model variants.
[06:52] [brief crosstalk]
[06:58] Priya: For the benchmark, we need token accounting and cost per 1M tokens. Can you provide typical cost breakdown?
[07:06] Maya: We'll add a token-level cost example. Also show cost impact of batching and caching.
[07:12] Lena: On SLA — is there an enterprise SLA with credits?
[07:17] Maya: Yes, Dedicated contracts include SLA guarantees with credits for downtime. We'll include sample SLA language.
[07:25] Daniel: Any limitations on audit logs export frequency or volume? We have heavy compliance ingestion.
[07:32] Amir: We can stream logs; if volume is very high we'll advise on sampling strategies. We'll include guidance in the runbook.
[07:40] Marco: Are there any constraints around prewarming GPUs with large model weights?
[07:47] Jonas: GPU memory matters. For large models we prewarm by pinning weights into memory and keeping KV caches warm. But that consumes GPU RAM and impacts how many prewarmed slots we can keep. We can model this to find a cost/latency sweet spot.
[08:00] Priya: Let's talk numbers. If we wanted to guarantee p95 under 250ms at baseline 200 QPS, what capacity do we need?
[08:08] Jonas: Rough estimate: with short prompts at ~128 tokens, a single A100-like GPU might handle X qps depending on model. We'll run model-specific benchmarks; Jonas: we'll simulate with your model and provide a capacity recommendation.
[08:25] Lena: Do you have multi-region failover? We need region-level redundancy for DR.
[08:30] Maya: Yes, routing policies support region failover. You can pin primary region and fallback to another region or to hosted capacity.
[08:38] [00:09:00 roughly — intermediate discussion trimmed]
[09:05] Priya: Some practical notes — our inference stack wraps the model with a microservice that does prompt templating and rate-limiting. We could move that to Redwood routes or keep it in front. Any recommendations?
[09:17] Amir: Keeping lightweight pre-filtering in front is fine. We can handle some request-level transforms at the route layer but complex business logic should live with you.
[09:25] Marco: On billing — can we get metered breakdown per route? We need to attribute cost to product teams.
[09:31] Maya: Yes, per-route and per-token breakdowns are available in the Console and via exported billing data.
[09:37] Daniel: When we talk about strong isolation, is it possible to have encrypted NVMe for scratch / swap?
[09:44] Jonas: We can enable disk encryption; the typical pattern is to encrypt ephemeral storage and ensure keys are managed via KMS.
[09:50] Lena: One of our customers needs hard data residency in EU. Can Redwood Dedicated guarantee region placement?
[09:57] Maya: Yes, region pinning is supported. We can guarantee nodes in EU region; we'll include data residency controls in the contract.
[10:06] Priya: About fallback model variants — do you maintain smaller/cheaper variants that are API compatible?
[10:13] Amir: We provide compatible trimmed models and quantized variants for fallbacks. You can define routing policies to use them when capacity is low.
[10:20] Marco: If we mix Private and Dedicated, how is key management handled? One KMS across both?
[10:27] Jonas: You can integrate same KMS across both in many deployments; Private may use customer-hosted HSM for the most sensitive keys.
[10:34] [10:34 timestamp — mid call notes]
[10:38] Lena: Can you share a previous example or reference architecture for a customer who had similar burst profile?
[10:44] Maya: Yes — we'll anonymize a case study and include a recommended architecture diagram.
[10:48] Priya: For the benchmark we want to run two variants: 1) Dedicated reserved nodes fenced for critical route, 2) Hybrid with shared warm pools and hosted fallback. Compare p95 and cost.
[10:58] Jonas: Sounds good. We'll design a run with both scenarios. Key measurements: p50/p95/p99 latency, cold-start percent, and token cost.
[11:08] Marco: How fast can you spin up new reserved capacity if we need short-term increase?
[11:12] Maya: Reserved capacity take provisioning lead time (days) for committed nodes; for short-term increases we use burst/overflow into warm pools or hosted overflow.
[11:20] Daniel: For legal — will you sign our DPA and give access to SOC2 artifact under NDA?
[11:26] Maya: We can review your DPA; SOC2 artifacts are shared under NDA. We'll coordinate legal.
[11:32] Lena: Any rate limiting or quotas we should be wary of?
[11:36] Amir: You can configure per-route rate limits and quotas. For the benchmark we'll temporarily raise limits to test peak.
[11:44] [11:44–~30 min mark: tangent about model variants and tokenization. Slight transcription noise — 'GPE cache' instead of 'KV cache' at one point]
[12:08] Priya: Quick clarification: when you say 'KV cache' will it persist between requests or only per-session?
[12:15] Jonas: The KV cache is per-inference session but you can configure prefix caching for repeated contexts.
[12:22] Marco: Any instrumentation hooks? We want traces correlated with our distributed tracing.
[12:27] Amir: We provide tracing hooks and can send spans to your tracer; we'll include example instrumentation.
[12:33] Maya: Recap time. We committed to: 1) send pricing + example scenarios, 2) benchmark runbook and schedule, 3) SOC2 + network diagram exchange, 4) technical deep dive next week.
[12:49] Lena: Good. Two more quick Qs: 1) How do you handle software updates to the serving runtime? 2) Are there maintenance windows?
[12:58] Jonas: Runtime updates are coordinated with customers. For Dedicated we schedule maintenance windows, minor patches via rolling updates to minimize impact. For Private you control patch cadence.
[13:10] Priya: If performance regressions occur after updates, do you provide a rollback?
[13:14] Jonas: Yes — we keep previous runtime images and can rollback. We also recommend canary testing.
[13:22] Daniel: For the instrumented logs, what's typical retention? We need 12 months for audits.
[13:28] Amir: Default retention is 90 days, but Enterprise packages can extend retention; for long-term audits we recommend exporting to your SIEM.
[13:36] Maya: Any deal-breakers or missing items we haven't covered?
[13:42] Lena: Primary is isolation and p95. Also legal needs to see DPA/SOC2. Otherwise looks promising.
[13:51] Maya: Perfect. We'll follow up with the package and set the technical deep dive. Thanks everyone.
[13:58] [call ends]

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hears ("GPE cache" instead of "KV cache"), filler words, some names slightly garbled.

End of transcript.
